claims.text: The initial W–Cu composite contains tungsten particles with native surface oxide layers.
The initial W–Cu composite has a continuous copper matrix.
Tungsten particles will be coated with a 10–20 nm Ag layer by PVD before consolidation.
The coated particles will be consolidated by spark plasma sintering at 800–900 °C under moderate pressure.
The stated coating and consolidation conditions mimic the high-heat-flux and irradiation environments of fusion-reactor joints.
The intervention will produce a conformal nanometric Ag interlayer at W/Cu interfaces.
The Ag interlayer will ensure robust metallurgical bonding between tungsten and copper.
The Ag nanolayer will enhance interfacial bonding.
The Ag nanolayer will act as an electronic bridge between the tungsten and copper phases.
The Ag nanolayer will decrease thermal boundary resistance at W/Cu interfaces.
Silver's intrinsic high thermal conductivity will aid electron transport through the composite.
Silver's stable metallurgical properties will help preserve the composite's mechanical integrity.
Silver's stable metallurgical properties will help preserve the composite's irradiation resistance.
The Ag-coated W–Cu composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable composite containing uncoated tungsten particles.
The Ag-coated composite will retain mechanical durability similar to that of the uncoated baseline.
The Ag-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance similar to that of the uncoated baseline.
The anticipated improvement will hold under fusion-reactor and high-heat-flux service conditions.
